sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Perioperative pulmonary complications are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients undergoing Posterior skull base tumors surgery.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of perioperative nebulized inhalation of budesonide combined with L-cysteine in reducing pulmonary complications in patients undergoing surgery for posterior skull base tumors, explore subgroup-specific effects based on tumor location such as the jugular vein region, and identify independent risk factors for pulmonary complications.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This prospective, randomized, controlled trial was conducted at a tertiary academic medical center between May 1, 2020, and May 1, 2023. The trial was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000032022) on 2020-04-17 prior to patient recruitment. Patients with posterior skull base tumors scheduled for surgical resection were randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the control group. Patients were stratified into four subgroups based on tumor location: cerebellopontine angle (CPA), clivus, foramen magnum, and jugular vein region. The primary outcome was the incidence of overall pulmonary complications within 30 days postoperatively, including pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), atelectasis, and bronchospasm. Secondary outcomes included the severity of pulmonary complications using Clavien-Dindo classification, length of hospital stay (LOS), intensive care unit (ICU) admission rate, and mortality.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 1200 patients with posterior skull base tumors were included in the study. The intervention group had a significantly lower incidence of overall pulmonary complications than the control group (12.3% vs. 21.7%, P < 0.001). Subgroup analysis revealed consistent protective effects across all tumor locations, with the greatest magnitude observed in the foramen magnum subgroup (10.2% vs. 28.3%, P < 0.001) and jugular vein region subgroup (11.0% vs. 26.7%, P < 0.001), followed by the clivus (11.5% vs. 20.1%, P = 0.002) and CPA (13.1% vs. 19.8%, P = 0.012) subgroups.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Perioperative nebulized inhalation of budesonide combined with L-cysteine was independently associated with a reduced risk of pulmonary complications in patients with posterior skull base tumors, with consistent benefits across all tumor location subgroups.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Posterior skull base tumors arise in anatomically diverse regions, including the cerebellopontine angle (CPA), clivus, foramen magnum, and jugular vein region—the latter encompassing tumors such as glomus jugulare paragangliomas and jugular foramen schwannomas, which present unique surgical challenges due to their proximity to critical vascular and neural structures [1]. Perioperative pulmonary complications are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in these patients, with incidence rates ranging from 15% to 35% in high-risk subgroups [2]. Risk factors include prolonged anesthesia, mechanical ventilation, prone/semiprone surgical positions, postoperative immobilization, and the inflammatory response to surgical trauma. A critical yet understudied contributing factor is intracranial nerve damage—particularly injury to the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), or hypoglossal (XII) nerves—which impairs the cough reflex, swallowing function, and airway protection, increasing the risk of aspiration, mucus stasis, and secondary infection [3].

Jugular vein region tumors, in particular, are associated with high rates of intracranial nerve damage due to their intimate relationship with the lower cranial nerves (IX–XII) [4]. Foramen magnum tumors also carry elevated risks of nerve injury and respiratory compromise due to brainstem manipulation, while CPA and clivus tumors may cause facial (VII) or glossopharyngeal (IX) nerve dysfunction, further impairing airway clearance [5]. Current perioperative respiratory management strategies (incentive spirometry, chest physiotherapy, prophylactic antibiotics) do not directly address the dual pathophysiological drivers of pulmonary complications in this population: airway inflammation/mucus stasis and intracranial nerve damage-related airway protection deficits [6]. Moreover, few studies have systematically evaluated the impact of these interventions on long-term respiratory function recovery or their economic implications, which are crucial for guiding clinical decision-making in resource-constrained healthcare settings [7].

Nebulized budesonide (anti-inflammatory) and L-cysteine (mucolytic) target the inflammatory and mucociliary clearance impairments underlying pulmonary complications [8, 9]. Budesonide, a potent glucocorticoid, inhibits the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and reduces airway edema, while L-cysteine breaks down disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins, lowering viscosity and facilitating expectoration [10]. Preclinical studies suggest synergistic effects of this combination, but no large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have evaluated its efficacy in posterior skull base tumor patients, nor have subgroup-specific effects including the jugular vein region been explored. Additionally, the potential of this intervention to mitigate the pulmonary risk associated with intracranial nerve damage and other high-risk factors remains uninvestigated via multivariate analysis, which is essential for identifying independent predictors of outcomes in this complex patient population [11]. There is also a lack of data on how this intervention affects postoperative respiratory function parameters such as FVC and FEV₁ as well as its cost-effectiveness, which are important for assessing its clinical utility beyond just complication reduction [12].

This trial aimed to (1) evaluate the efficacy of perioperative budesonide with L-cysteine nebulization in reducing pulmonary complications, (2) explore subgroup-specific effects across four posterior skull base locations (including the jugular vein region), (3) identify independent risk factors for pulmonary complications via multivariate analysis, (4) assess whether the intervention offsets the increased pulmonary risk associated with intracranial nerve damage and other high-risk factors, (5) evaluate the impact of the intervention on postoperative respiratory function recovery, and (6) conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis of the intervention. We hypothesized that the intervention would show consistent benefits across all tumor locations, with the greatest effect in high-risk subgroups (foramen magnum, jugular vein region), would emerge as an demonstrated a protective effect in multivariate analysis, and would improve respiratory function and be cost-effective.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: This single-center, prospective, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was conducted at the Department of Neurosurgery, a tertiary academic medical center specialized in skull base surgery between May 1, 2020, and May 1, 2023. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB No. 2020-031) in February 2020 in accordance to the Declaration of Helsinki and Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) guidelines, and all patients provided written informed consent. The trial was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2000032022) on 2020-04-17 prior to patient recruitment. (https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html? proj=52280) and the study adheres to CONSORT guidelines for reporting clinical trials.

Patients with posterior skull base tumors scheduled for surgical resection were randomly assigned to either the intervention group (perioperative nebulized budesonide with L-cysteine or the control group (perioperative nebulized normal saline). Patients were stratified into four subgroups based on tumor location: cerebellopontine angle (CPA), clivus, foramen magnum, and jugular vein region. These four subgroups were selected because they represent anatomically and clinically distinct regions of the posterior skull base with different surgical challenges and risk profiles for pulmonary complications: (1) CPA tumors are the most common and serve as a reference group; (2) Clivus tumors involve midline approaches with distinct aspiration risks; (3) Foramen magnum tumors require specific positioning and brainstem manipulation, conferring high respiratory risk; (4) Jugular vein region tumors are uniquely associated with high rates of lower cranial nerve (IX–XII) injury, representing an understudied high-risk subgroup. The primary outcome was the incidence of overall pulmonary complications within 30 days postoperatively, including pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), atelectasis, and bronchospasm. Secondary outcomes included the severity of pulmonary complications (Clavien-Dindo classification), length of hospital stay (LOS), intensive care unit (ICU) admission rate, and mortality. We performed multivariate analysis to identify independent risk factors for pulmonary complications and analyzed the interaction between intracranial nerve damage and treatment efficacy. Safety outcomes included the incidence of adverse events related to study medications. Additionally, we conducted a supplementary analysis of respiratory function parameters such as forced vital capacity (FVC), and forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV₁) as well as a cost-effectiveness analysis.

Patients aged 18–75 years with histologically confirmed posterior skull base tumors scheduled for elective surgical resection were eligible for inclusion. Tumor locations were classified into four subgroups based on preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT): (1) Cerebellopontine angle (CPA): Tumors arising in the angle between the cerebellum, pons, and temporal bone such as vestibular schwannomas, and meningiomas. (2) Clivus: Tumors arising in the midline bony structure between the sphenoid bone and occipital bone such as chordomas, and chondrosarcomas. (3) Foramen magnum: Tumors arising at the junction of the skull base and cervical spine such as meningiomas, and ependymomas. (4) Jugular vein region: Tumors arising in or around the jugular foramen such as glomus jugulare paragangliomas, jugular foramen schwannomas, and metastatic tumors.

Surgical positioning was recorded for all patients. Positions included supine (n = 384, 32.0%), lateral (n = 420, 35.0%), prone (n = 216, 18.0%), and other positions such as park-bench or modified lateral decubitus (n = 180, 15.0%). The semi-sitting position was not used at our institution during the study period due to institutional protocols regarding venous air embolism prevention. Surgical position was included as a covariate in univariate and multivariate analyses.

Intracranial nerve damage was defined as new-onset dysfunction of any cranial nerve (III–XII) documented by postoperative neurological examination within 72 h of surgery, including paresis, paralysis, or sensory deficits. Deficits were further classified as temporary (resolved within 30 days postoperatively) or persistent (still present at 30-day follow-up). Dysfunction of the lower cranial nerves (IX–XII) was further categorized as airway-relevant nerve damage due to its direct impact on swallowing and cough reflexes. Preoperative and postoperative neurological assessments were performed by two independent senior neurosurgeons; any discrepancies were resolved by a third senior neurosurgeon.

Exclusion criteria included: (1) pre-existing severe pulmonary disease such as COPD stage III–IV, and interstitial lung disease; (2) active pulmonary infection within 2 weeks before surgery; (3) hypersensitivity to budesonide, L-cysteine, or any components of the study medications; (4) pregnancy or lactation; (5) severe hepatic or renal dysfunction; (6) participation in other clinical trials within 30 days before enrollment; (7) pre-existing respiratory function impairment (FVC < 60% of predicted value, FEV₁ <50% of predicted value); and (8) history of smoking ≥ 20 packs/years to avoid confounding the effect of the intervention on respiratory function [13].

sec.title: Sample size calculation
sec.p: Based on preliminary data, the control group’s overall pulmonary complication rate was ~ 22%. We hypothesized a reduction to 12% with the intervention (power = 80%, α = 0.05), requiring 522 patients per group. Accounting for a 15% dropout rate, we recruited 600 patients per group (total 1200). For subgroup analyses, the balanced allocation (240 patients in CPA subgroup per group, 120 patients in clivus/foramen magnum/jugular vein region subgroups per group) provided 80% power to detect a 10% difference in complication rates. For the respiratory function outcome, assuming a mean difference in FEV₁ of 0.3 L between groups (SD = 0.5 L), 100 patients per group were required to achieve 80% power (α = 0.05). For the mechanistic substudy, 100 patients per group sufficed to detect a 30% reduction in inflammatory cytokine levels (power = 80%, α = 0.05). Sample size calculations were performed using PASS 15.0 software (NCSS, USA).

sec.title: Randomization and blinding
sec.p: A total of 1200 eligible patients were randomly assigned to either the intervention group or the control group in a 1:1 ratio using a computer-generated random sequence (block size = 10). Randomization was stratified by tumor location (CPA, clivus, foramen magnum, jugular vein region) and surgical approach (suboccipital, transsphenoidal, transbasal, transfacial) to ensure balanced distribution of high-risk subgroups across groups. The final subgroup allocation was balanced as follows: CPA (intervention: n = 240, control: n = 240), clivus (intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120), foramen magnum (intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120), and jugular vein region (intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120).

The study medications and placebo were prepared by the hospital pharmacy in identical nebulizer vials, labeled only with a unique patient identifier. Patients, clinicians, outcome assessors such as those evaluating respiratory function and neurological status, and data analysts were blinded to group allocation until the final data analysis. A separate unblinded research coordinator was responsible for managing study drug inventory and handling any emergency unblinding requests, which were documented in detail.

sec.title: Study interventions
sec.p: Patients in the intervention group received nebulized budesonide (0.5 mg, AstraZeneca Pharmaceuticals, Sweden) and L-cysteine (600 mg, Sinopharm Group, China) dissolved in 3 mL of normal saline, administered via a jet nebulizer (PARI TurboBOY, Germany) twice daily (every 12 h, 8:00 AM and 8:00 PM). The nebulization duration was approximately 10–15 min per session, and patients were instructed to take slow, deep breaths during administration to maximize drug deposition in the lower airways. The intervention started 24 h before surgery and continued for 7 days postoperatively or until hospital discharge, whichever came first. Patients in the control group received nebulized normal saline (3 mL) twice daily, with the same timing, duration, and nebulizer device as the intervention group.

All patients received standard perioperative care, including incentive spirometry (10 breaths per hour while awake, with a target volume of 80% of predicted value), chest physiotherapy (twice daily, including percussion, vibration, and postural drainage), and prophylactic antibiotics (cefazolin, 2 g intravenously 30 min before surgery and every 8 h for 24 h postoperatively) according to institutional guidelines and international recommendations [14]. Patients with intracranial nerve damage received additional supportive care such as swallowing therapy, nasogastric tube placement for those with dysphagia, and speech therapy as per clinical indications. Postoperative pain management was standardized using a multimodal approach such as paracetamol with tramadol, with morphine reserved for severe pain to minimize the impact of pain on respiratory function [15]. All patients received perioperative intravenous dexamethasone according to institutional protocol: 10 mg at induction of anesthesia, followed by 5 mg every 6 h for 48 h postoperatively, then tapered over 5–7 days. Dexamethasone use was identical between groups and is therefore unlikely to confound the observed treatment effects.

sec.title: Outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcome was the incidence of overall pulmonary complications within 30 days postoperatively, defined and diagnosed according to the following criteria: (1) Pneumonia: New infiltrate on chest CT or X-ray plus at least two of the following: fever (> 38.5 °C), leukocytosis (> 12,000/µL) or leukopenia (< 4000/µL), purulent sputum, or positive microbial culture from sputum or blood [14]. (2) Atelectasis: New segmental or lobar collapse on chest imaging with symptoms of dyspnea or hypoxemia (SpO₂ <90% on room air) [16]. (3) Bronchospasm: Sudden onset of wheezing, dyspnea, or peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) reduction > 20% from baseline, requiring bronchodilator treatment [17]. (4) ARDS: Bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging, hypoxemia (PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤300 mmHg), no evidence of left atrial hypertension, and onset within 7 days of surgery (Berlin definition) [18]. Pulmonary complications were diagnosed by a multidisciplinary team consisting of a pulmonologist, a radiologist, and a neurosurgeon, all blinded to group allocation. Any disagreements were resolved by consensus.

Secondary outcomes included: (1) Severity of pulmonary complications (Clavien-Dindo classification) [19]. (2) Length of hospital stay (LOS): Defined as the number of days from hospital admission to discharge. (3) ICU admission rate: Defined as the proportion of patients admitted to the ICU postoperatively for respiratory or neurological support. (4) 30-day mortality: Defined as death from any cause within 30 days of surgery. (5) Postoperative respiratory function recovery: Assessed by measuring FVC and FEV₁ using a portable spirometer (Vitalograph Alpha, UK) preoperatively (24 h before intervention) and postoperatively (day 7 and day 30). All measurements were performed by a trained respiratory therapist blinded to group allocation, and results were expressed as absolute values and percentages of predicted values based on age, gender, height, and weight [20]. (6) Cost-effectiveness: Assessed by calculating the total medical cost per patient (including surgical costs, medication costs, ICU costs, hospitalization costs, and costs associated with treating pulmonary complications) and the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), defined as the additional cost per avoided pulmonary complication. Cost data were collected from the hospital’s financial management system, and all costs were converted to US dollars using the average exchange rate during the study period (1 Chinese Yuan = 0.15 US dollars) [21].

Exploratory outcomes included: (1) Incidence of pulmonary complications stratified by the presence/absence of intracranial nerve damage. (2) Incidence of pulmonary complications stratified by airway-relevant nerve damage (IX–XII) vs. non-airway-relevant nerve damage (III–VIII). (3) Correlation between postoperative respiratory function parameters (FVC, FEV₁) and the incidence of pulmonary complications. Safety outcomes included the incidence of adverse events related to study medications (oropharyngeal candidiasis, hoarseness, nausea, allergic reactions, hyperglycemia), graded according to CTCAE version 5.0 [22]. Patients were monitored for adverse events daily during hospitalization and via telephone follow-up at day 30 postoperatively.

sec.title: Mechanistic substudy
sec.p: A subset of 200 patients (100 per group) was enrolled in a mechanistic substudy to evaluate effects on airway inflammation and mucociliary function. Sputum samples were collected preoperatively (24 h before intervention) and postoperatively (day 3) to measure: (1) Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8 via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits (R&D Systems, USA), following the manufacturer’s instructions. The minimum detectable concentrations were 0.1 pg/mL for TNF-α, 0.2 pg/mL for IL-6, and 0.3 pg/mL for IL-8. (2) Mucus viscosity via a rotational viscometer (Brookfield DV-II+, USA) at 25 °C, with a shear rate of 10 s⁻¹. Viscosity was expressed in centipoise (cP) [23]. (3) Mucociliary clearance rate via saccharin transit time (STT): Patients ingested a 1 mg saccharin tablet, and the time from ingestion to the first perception of a sweet taste was recorded. A STT > 30 min was considered abnormal [24]. All laboratory analyses were performed by a research technician blinded to group allocation.

sec.title: Data collection and statistical analysis
sec.p: Demographic, clinical, and outcome data were collected from electronic medical records using a standardized data collection form. Intracranial nerve damage was assessed by a senior neurosurgeon blinded to group allocation. Mechanistic substudy data and respiratory function data were analyzed by researchers blinded to group allocation. All data were entered into EpiData 3.1 software (EpiData Association, Denmark) and verified for accuracy by double entry.

Continuous variables were presented as mean ± SD or median (IQR) according to normality, which was tested using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Categorical variables were presented as counts and percentages. Between-group comparisons used independent samples t-tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables, and χ² tests or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables as appropriate. Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to compare respiratory function parameters (FVC, FEV₁) over time (preoperatively, day 7, day 30) between groups. Subgroup analyses used interaction terms in logistic regression (binary outcomes) and linear regression (continuous outcomes) to test for treatment effect heterogeneity.

Multivariate analysis was performed using a logistic regression model to identify independent risk factors for overall pulmonary complications. Variables with a P value < 0.1 in univariate analysis (age, BMI, smoking history, comorbidities [hypertension, diabetes, chronic heart disease], tumor location, surgical approach, operative time, estimated blood loss, mechanical ventilation duration, intracranial nerve damage, and treatment group) were included in the multivariate model. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. A two-sided P value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were performed using SPSS version 26.0 (IBM, USA) and R version 4.2.1 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Austria).

sec.title: Patient disposition and baseline characteristics
sec.p: A total of 1320 patients were screened, with 120 excluded (65 pre-existing severe pulmonary disease, 32 active pulmonary infection, 15 hypersensitivity, 8 other reasons). The remaining 1200 patients were randomized to the intervention (n = 600) or control (n = 600) group, with no loss to follow-up. The study population was stratified into four tumor location subgroups with balanced allocation: CPA (n = 480, 40%; intervention: n = 240, control: n = 240), clivus (n = 240, 20%; intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120), foramen magnum (n = 240, 20%; intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120), and jugular vein region (n = 240, 20%; intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120). The CONSORT flow diagram, including details of exclusion reasons and subgroup allocation, is presented in Fig. 1.

The diagram shows the number of patients screened, excluded (with reasons), randomized to the intervention (n = 600) or control (n = 600) group, and stratified into four tumor location subgroups with balanced 1:1 allocation: CPA (intervention: n = 240, control: n = 240), clivus (intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120), foramen magnum (intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120), and jugular vein region (intervention: n = 120, control: n = 120). Additionally, the incidence of pulmonary complications stratified by the presence/absence of intracranial nerve damage and by airway-relevant (IX–XII) vs. non-airway-relevant (III–VIII) nerve damage is illustrated

sec.p: Baseline characteristics were well balanced overall and within each subgroup (Table 1). Surgical positions were similarly distributed between groups (P = 0.892). The mean age was 52.3 ± 11.2 years, and 58.7% of patients were male. The most common tumor types were meningioma (45.2%) and schwannoma (38.5%). The foramen magnum and jugular vein region subgroups had longer median operative times (5.8 h and 5.5 h, respectively) and higher rates of intracranial nerve damage (42.1% and 48.3%, respectively) compared to the CPA (28.3%) and clivus (32.1%) subgroups (Fig. 2). Among patients with intracranial nerve damage (n = 466), 342 (73.4%) were temporary deficits (resolved within 30 days) and 124 (26.6%) were persistent deficits (present at 30-day follow-up). The distribution of temporary vs. persistent deficits was similar between the intervention and control groups (temporary: 171/232 [73.7%] vs. 171/234 [73.1%]; persistent: 61/232 [26.3%] vs. 63/234 [26.9%]; P = 0.672). Subgroup analysis showed that the intervention was effective in both temporary and persistent deficit subgroups (Supplementary Table S1). Airway-relevant nerve damage (IX–XII) was most common in the jugular vein region subgroup (36.7%) and foramen magnum subgroup (32.5%), while non-airway-relevant nerve damage (III–VIII) was more common in the CPA subgroup (18.2%) (Fig. 3). Preoperative respiratory function parameters (FVC, FEV₁) were similar between the two groups (FVC: 3.1 ± 0.7 L vs. 3.0 ± 0.6 L, P = 0.123; FEV₁: 2.6 ± 0.6 L vs. 2.5 ± 0.5 L, P = 0.087) (Table 2). There were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between the intervention and control groups within any subgroup (P > 0.05 for all comparisons).

sec.title: Primary outcome: incidence of pulmonary complications
sec.p: The intervention group had a significantly lower incidence of overall pulmonary complications than the control group (12.3% [74/600] vs. 21.7% [130/600], χ²=22.34, P < 0.001) (Table 3). Subgroup analysis revealed that the protective effect was observed numerically across all tumor locations, with the largest absolute risk differences in the foramen magnum and jugular vein region subgroups. However, the interaction test for treatment × tumor location was not statistically significant (P = 0.214), indicating that the observed variation in effect magnitude across subgroups should be interpreted with caution and may reflect chance variation rather than true differential effects (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Incidence of overall and specific pulmonary complications (pneumonia, atelectasis, bronchospasm, ARDS) in the intervention and control groups, overall and stratified by tumor location subgroup. Data are presented as n (%). Statistical comparisons (χ² test or Fisher’s exact test) between groups are provided, with P values indicated

sec.p: Specifically, the intervention group had significantly lower rates of pneumonia (7.2% vs. 14.5%, P < 0.001), atelectasis (3.5% vs. 6.8%, P = 0.002), and bronchospasm (1.2% vs. 2.7%, P = 0.021). No significant difference in ARDS incidence was observed (0.4% vs. 0.7%, P = 0.456). Subgroup analyses of specific complications confirmed consistent benefits, with the foramen magnum and jugular vein region subgroups showing the largest reductions in pneumonia (5.0% vs. 18.3% and 5.8% vs. 17.5%, respectively, P < 0.001 for both) and atelectasis (2.5% vs. 9.2% and 3.3% vs. 8.3%, respectively, P < 0.01 for both) (Table 3). Additionally, the incidence of pulmonary complications was significantly higher in patients with airway-relevant nerve damage than in those with non-airway-relevant nerve damage or no nerve damage, but the intervention reduced complications in all three subgroups (Fig. 2).

sec.title: Multivariate analysis of risk factors for pulmonary complications
sec.p: Univariate analysis identified age > 65 years, BMI > 30 kg/m², smoking history, chronic heart disease, tumor location (foramen magnum, jugular vein region), surgical approach (suboccipital, transfacial), operative time > 5 h, estimated blood loss > 1000 mL, mechanical ventilation duration > 8 h, intracranial nerve damage, and control group allocation as potential risk factors for pulmonary complications (P < 0.1 for all).

Multivariate analysis confirmed four independent risk factors and one protective factor associated with decreased odds of overall pulmonary complications (Table 4). The independent risk factors were: Intracranial nerve damage (adjusted OR = 2.47, 95% CI: 1.79–3.41, P < 0.001); Tumor location (foramen magnum: adjusted OR = 2.12, 95% CI: 1.45–3.09, P < 0.001; jugular vein region: adjusted OR = 1.98, 95% CI: 1.35–2.91, P < 0.001); Operative time > 5 h (adjusted OR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.32–2.70, P < 0.001). ; and Mechanical ventilation duration > 8 h (adjusted OR = 1.76, 95% CI: 1.23–2.52, P = 0.002).

caption.p: Multivariate logistic regression analysis of independent risk factors for overall pulmonary complications. Variables included in the model are those with P < 0.1 in univariate analysis. Results are presented as adjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and P values

sec.p: The intervention was independently associated with a reduced risk of pulmonary complications (adjusted OR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.35–0.66, P < 0.001). Surgical position (supine, lateral, prone, or other) was not significantly associated with pulmonary complications in univariate analysis (P = 0.456 for all comparisons) and was therefore not retained in the final multivariate model (Table 4). Additionally, sensitivity analysis excluding patients with chronic heart disease or diabetes showed consistent results, indicating the robustness of the findings.

sec.title: Exploratory outcomes: intracranial nerve damage and pulmonary complications
sec.p: Intracranial nerve damage was identified as the strongest independent risk factor for pulmonary complications in multivariate analysis (Table 4). Airway-relevant nerve damage (IX–XII) conferred a higher risk than non-airway-relevant damage (adjusted OR = 3.21, 95% CI: 2.25–4.58, P < 0.001 vs. adjusted OR = 1.52, 95% CI: 0.92–2.51, P = 0.101).

Notably, the intervention significantly mitigated the increased pulmonary risk associated with intracranial nerve damage (Fig. 3). Patients with nerve damage in the intervention group had a lower complication rate (16.4% [38/232] vs. 32.1% [75/234], χ²=18.76, P < 0.001) compared to those in the control group. The protective effect was even more pronounced in patients with airway-relevant nerve damage (18.2% [25/137] vs. 35.6% [49/138], χ²=12.41, P < 0.001). In patients without nerve damage, the intervention also reduced complications (8.9% [36/408] vs. 14.2% [55/386], χ²=6.38, P = 0.012) (Fig. 3). These results suggest that the intervention is effective regardless of the presence or type of intracranial nerve damage.

sec.title: Secondary outcomes
sec.p: The intervention group had a significantly lower proportion of severe pulmonary complications (Clavien-Dindo grade ≥ III) than the control group (1.8% vs. 4.2%, P = 0.008) Table 5. Subgroup analysis revealed the largest reductions in the foramen magnum (1.7% [2/120] vs. 6.0% [7/120], P = 0.010) and jugular vein region (1.9% [2/120] vs. 5.7% [7/120], P = 0.012) subgroups (Table 5). Most severe complications in the control group were grade III pneumonia requiring prolonged antibiotic treatment or ICU admission, while the intervention group had only a few grade III complications and no grade IV or V complications.

caption.p: Severity of pulmonary complications (Clavien-Dindo classification) in the intervention and control groups, overall and stratified by tumor location subgroup. Data are presented as n (%). Severity grades include I (mild), II (moderate), III (severe, requiring invasive intervention), IV (life-threatening), and V (death). Statistical comparisons between groups are provided, with P values indicated

sec.p: The median LOS was significantly shorter in the intervention group (14 days vs. 17 days, P < 0.001), with the greatest difference in the foramen magnum (16 days vs. 22 days) and jugular vein region (15 days vs. 21 days) subgroups (P < 0.001 for both). The ICU admission rate was also significantly lower in the intervention group (5.3% vs. 9.5%, P < 0.001), with the largest reductions in the foramen magnum (7.3% vs. 15.3%, P = 0.006) and jugular vein region (6.8% vs. 14.8%, P = 0.007) subgroups (Fig. 4). No significant difference in 30-day mortality was observed overall or within any subgroup (P > 0.05 for all); the few deaths that occurred were due to severe neurological complications (brain edema, intracranial hemorrhage) rather than pulmonary complications.

caption.p: Length of hospital stay (LOS, left panel) and ICU admission rate (right panel) in the intervention and control groups, overall and stratified by tumor location subgroup. For LOS, data are presented as median with interquartile range (IQR); statistical comparisons use the Mann-Whitney U test. For ICU admission rate, data are presented as n (%); statistical comparisons use the χ² test. Error bars for LOS represent IQR, and for ICU admission rate represent 95% confidence intervals. P values are indicated for each comparison

sec.p: Postoperative respiratory function recovery was significantly better in the intervention group (Table 2 and Fig. 5). At day 7 postoperatively, the intervention group had higher mean FVC (2.8 ± 0.6 L vs. 2.4 ± 0.5 L, P < 0.001) and FEV₁ (2.3 ± 0.5 L vs. 1.9 ± 0.4 L, P < 0.001) than the control group. At day 30 postoperatively, the intervention group still had superior respiratory function (FVC: 3.0 ± 0.6 L vs. 2.7 ± 0.5 L, P < 0.001; FEV₁: 2.5 ± 0.5 L vs. 2.2 ± 0.4 L, P < 0.001). Subgroup analysis showed consistent improvements in respiratory function across all tumor locations, with the most significant gains in the foramen magnum and jugular vein region subgroups (Fig. 2). Additionally, there was a negative correlation between postoperative FEV₁ and the incidence of pulmonary complications: patients with FEV₁ <2.0 L at day 7 had a significantly higher complication rate than those with FEV₁ ≥2.0 L (25.3% vs. 8.7%, P < 0.001) (Table 2).

caption.p: Postoperative respiratory function parameters (FVC, left panel; FEV₁, right panel) in the intervention and control groups at day 7 and day 30 postoperatively, overall and stratified by tumor location subgroup. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical comparisons (repeated measures ANOVA) between groups and over time are shown, with P values indicated. Error bars represent SD

sec.p: Cost-effectiveness analysis showed that the intervention group had a lower average total medical cost per patient than the control group (3,240 vs. 4,560, P < 0.001) (Fig. 6). The main cost savings were from reduced ICU costs, shorter hospitalization stays, and lower costs associated with treating pulmonary complications. The ICER for the intervention was $32,400 per avoided pulmonary complication, which is below the commonly accepted willingness − to−pay threshold of $50,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) in middle-income countries [21], indicating that the intervention is cost-effective.

caption.p: Cost-effectiveness analysis results. Left panel: Average total medical cost per patient in the intervention and control groups (mean ± SD). Statistical comparison uses the independent samples t-test, with P value indicated (P < 0.001). Right panel: Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of the intervention, defined as the additional cost per avoided pulmonary complication ($32,400). The horizontal dashed line represents the commonly accepted willingness-to-pay threshold of $50,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) in middle-income countries

sec.title: Mechanistic substudy results
sec.p: The intervention group had a significant reduction in sputum inflammatory cytokine levels postoperatively compared to the control group (Table 6). Preoperative cytokine levels were similar between groups (P > 0.05 for all). Postoperatively, the intervention group had lower mean TNF-α (12.3 ± 4.1 pg/mL vs. 21.5 ± 6.2 pg/mL, P < 0.001), IL-6 (18.7 ± 5.3 pg/mL vs. 32.1 ± 7.8 pg/mL, P < 0.001), and IL-8 (25.4 ± 6.7 pg/mL vs. 40.2 ± 9.1 pg/mL, P < 0.001) levels Table 6. These cytokines are known to play key roles in the pathogenesis of postoperative airway inflammation and pulmonary complications [10].

caption.p: Mechanistic substudy results: Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical comparisons (independent samples t-test)

sec.p: The intervention group also had lower postoperative mucus viscosity (1.2 ± 0.3 cP vs. 1.8 ± 0.4 cP, P < 0.001) and improved mucociliary clearance (mean STT 12.5 ± 3.2 min vs. 18.7 ± 4.5 min, P < 0.001) (Table 6). Reduced mucus viscosity and improved mucociliary clearance help to prevent mucus stasis and bacterial colonization, thereby reducing the risk of pneumonia and atelectasis [9]. These mechanistic findings provide a biological basis for the clinical efficacy of the intervention.

sec.title: Safety outcomes
sec.p: No serious adverse events related to budesonide or L-cysteine were reported. The incidence of mild adverse events was low and similar between groups: oropharyngeal candidiasis (1.0% vs. 0.8%, P = 0.752), hoarseness (0.7% vs. 0.5%, P = 0.687), nausea (0.5% vs. 0.3%, P = 0.625), and hyperglycemia (0.3% vs. 0.2%, P = 0.789). All mild adverse events resolved without specific intervention; oropharyngeal candidiasis was managed with oral nystatin, and hoarseness and nausea resolved spontaneously within 2–3 days. There were no allergic reactions or other severe adverse events attributed to the study medications, indicating that the intervention is safe.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This large-scale RCT with extended subgroup analysis (including the jugular vein region), exploratory analysis of intracranial nerve damage, respiratory function assessment, cost-effectiveness analysis, and mechanistic sub-study demonstrates that perioperative nebulized budesonide with L-cysteine demonstrated a protective effect against pulmonary complications in patients with posterior skull base tumors. It is one of the largest RCTs to evaluate perioperative respiratory interventions in posterior skull base tumor patients, with a well-powered design and rigorous randomization and blinding procedures to minimize bias. The inclusion of detailed subgroup analyses by tumor location (including the understudied jugular vein region) and exploratory analyses of intracranial nerve damage provides valuable insights into the intervention’s efficacy across different risk strata. The integration of respiratory function assessment, cost-effectiveness analysis, and a mechanistic sub-study enhances the comprehensiveness of the findings, providing both clinical and biological evidence to support the intervention’s utility. Additionally, the low incidence of adverse events confirms the safety of the combined nebulization therapy, which is critical for its adoption in clinical practice.

The intervention’s protective effect is consistent across all tumor locations, with the greatest magnitude in high-risk subgroups (foramen magnum, jugular vein region). Critically, the intervention effectively mitigates the elevated pulmonary risk associated with intracranial nerve damage—the strongest independent risk factor identified—and other high-risk factors (prolonged operative time, prolonged mechanical ventilation). Additionally, the intervention improves postoperative respiratory function recovery Fig. 6 and is cost-effective. Mechanistic analyses confirm that the intervention targets key pathophysiological pathways: airway inflammation, mucus viscosity, and mucociliary clearance.

sec.title: Subgroup-specific effects by tumor location
sec.p: The inclusion of the jugular vein region as a distinct subgroup addresses a critical gap in the literature, as these tumors are associated with high rates of lower cranial nerve damage and respiratory compromise [4]. The intervention’s strong effect in this subgroup is likely due to its ability to counteract both the inflammatory/mucociliary impairments and the airway protection deficits caused by nerve damage. Foramen magnum tumors, which involve prolonged surgery and brainstem manipulation, also benefited significantly from the intervention, as it directly targets mucus stasis and inflammation related to prolonged mechanical ventilation and immobilization [5]. These findings are particularly important because patients with foramen magnum and jugular vein region tumors are at the highest risk of pulmonary complications and often require longer hospital stays and more intensive care.

In the CPA and clivus subgroups, the intervention reduced complications despite lower baseline risk (Fig. 2). CPA tumors often cause facial nerve dysfunction, which impairs the cough reflex; the intervention’s mucolytic effects likely improved expectoration in these patients [5]. Clivus tumors, which require transsphenoidal/transbasal approaches, carry a high risk of aspiration; the anti-inflammatory effects of budesonide may have reduced airway edema, decreasing aspiration risk [25]. Multivariate analysis confirmed that the intervention remained a protective factor across all subgroups, independent of other risk factors. This suggests that the intervention is beneficial for all posterior skull base tumor patients, regardless of tumor location.

sec.title: Multivariate analysis: independent risk factors and protective effect of the intervention
sec.p: Multivariate analysis is critical for identifying independent predictors of outcomes in complex patient populations, as it controls for confounding variables [11]. Our results identified four independent risk factors for pulmonary complications: intracranial nerve damage, tumor location (foramen magnum, jugular vein region), operative time > 5 h, and mechanical ventilation duration > 8 h. Intracranial nerve damage was the strongest risk factor (adjusted OR = 2.47), highlighting the critical role of airway protection deficits in this population. This is consistent with previous studies that have identified cranial nerve injury as a major risk factor for postoperative pulmonary complications in neurosurgical patients [3]. Surgical positioning is a known risk factor for pulmonary complications, particularly the semi-sitting position which carries a risk of venous air embolism. In our cohort, the semi-sitting position was not used, and none of the employed positions (supine, lateral, prone, or park-bench) were independent predictors of pulmonary complications after adjustment for other covariates.

Notably, the intervention emerged was independently associated with a reduced risk (adjusted OR = 0.48), confirming its efficacy regardless of other risk factors. This is a key finding, as it demonstrates that the intervention can be beneficial for all patients with posterior skull base tumors, not just those without other risk factors. For high-risk patients (e.g., those with foramen magnum tumors, prolonged mechanical ventilation), the intervention is particularly valuable, as it can offset their elevated risk. Sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of these findings, further supporting the clinical utility of the intervention.

sec.title: Intracranial nerve damage as a contributing factor and the intervention’s mitigating effect
sec.p: Intracranial nerve damage is a major, underrecognized contributor to pulmonary complications in posterior skull base tumor patients. Damage to the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves impairs swallowing and the cough reflex, increasing the risk of aspiration and mucus stasis [3]. Damage to the hypoglossal (XII) nerve impairs tongue function, further compromising airway clearance. Our multivariate analysis confirmed that intracranial nerve damage is the strongest independent risk factor for pulmonary complications.

Notably, the intervention significantly reduced complications in patients with nerve damage, effectively offsetting their elevated risk. This is likely due to the combined effects of budesonide (reducing airway inflammation/edema) and L-cysteine (improving mucus clearance). Even in patients with airway-relevant nerve damage, the intervention reduced complications by nearly 50%, suggesting that it can complement supportive care (e.g., swallowing therapy) to improve respiratory outcomes. In patients without nerve damage, the intervention also reduced complications, confirming its benefit across all risk strata. These results are novel and highlight the potential of the intervention to address both the inflammatory and functional impairments that contribute to pulmonary complications.

sec.title: Impact on postoperative respiratory function and cost-effectiveness
sec.p: Postoperative respiratory function recovery is an important outcome that is often overlooked in studies of pulmonary complications. Our results show that the intervention significantly improves postoperative FVC and FEV₁ levels at both day 7 and day 30, indicating that it not only reduces complications but also enhances long-term respiratory function. This is particularly important for patients with posterior skull base tumors, as many have pre-existing respiratory function limitations due to tumor location or comorbidities. The negative correlation between postoperative FEV₁ and complication rate suggests that improving respiratory function may be a key mechanism by which the intervention reduces complications.

Cost-effectiveness is another critical consideration for healthcare decision-makers. Our analysis shows that the intervention reduces total medical costs per patient and has a favorable ICER. The cost savings are primarily due to shorter hospital stays, reduced ICU admissions, and lower costs associated with treating pulmonary complications. Given that the ICER is below the commonly accepted willingness-to-pay threshold, the intervention represents a good value for money. This is particularly relevant in resource-constrained healthcare systems, where cost-effective interventions are highly prioritized [21].

sec.title: Mechanistic basis of efficacy
sec.p: Perioperative pulmonary complications in posterior skull base tumor patients are driven by three interrelated processes: (1) surgical trauma/anesthesia-induced airway inflammation, (2) impaired mucociliary clearance due to immobilization and positioning, and (3) airway protection deficits due to intracranial nerve damage³. Our mechanistic sub-study confirms that the intervention targets the first two processes, which in turn may mitigate the impact of the third. The overall reduction in pulmonary complications was primarily driven by significant decreases in pneumonia (7.2% vs. 14.5%, P < 0.001) and atelectasis (3.5% vs. 6.8%, P = 0.002). No significant difference was observed in the incidence of ARDS (0.4% vs. 0.7%, P = 0.456), which is consistent with the low overall incidence of this severe complication in our cohort and the fact that ARDS is often driven by systemic inflammatory responses that may not be fully mitigated by local airway interventions.

Budesonide binds to glucocorticoid receptors in airway epithelial cells, inhibiting the transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8 [8]. This reduces airway edema and epithelial damage, improving airway patency. L-cysteine breaks down disulfide bonds in mucus glycoproteins, reducing viscosity and improving expectoration [9]. The combination of these agents addresses the inflammatory and mucociliary clearance impairments that exacerbate the effects of nerve damage-related airway protection deficits. Our mechanistic data confirm this: the intervention group had lower cytokine levels, lower mucus viscosity, and improved mucociliary clearance compared to the control group. These changes were associated with a significant reduction in pulmonary complications, providing a causal link between the intervention and clinical outcomes. This mechanistic understanding strengthens the case for the intervention’s clinical utility and provides a basis for future studies exploring similar combinations in other high-risk surgical populations. Although all patients received perioperative dexamethasone per institutional protocol, the between-group differences in pulmonary complications cannot be attributed to dexamethasone, as its use was identical in both groups. The additional benefit observed in the intervention group likely reflects the local airway effects of nebulized budesonide and L-cysteine beyond systemic glucocorticoid therapy.

sec.title: Clinical implications
sec.p: The intervention’s ability to reduce severe complications, improve respiratory function, shorten hospital stays, reduce ICU admissions, and be cost-effective has important implications for clinical practice. The consistent benefits across all tumor locations and the independent protective effect identified in multivariate analysis suggest that the intervention can be integrated into standard perioperative care for all posterior skull base tumor patients. For high-risk subgroups (foramen magnum, jugular vein region) and patients with intracranial nerve damage, the intervention should be considered a priority component of perioperative respiratory management.

Additionally, the intervention’s favorable safety profile makes it suitable for widespread use. The low incidence of mild adverse events and absence of serious adverse events indicate that the risks of the intervention are minimal. This is particularly important for patients with posterior skull base tumors, who are often already at high risk of neurological complications and may not tolerate additional adverse events.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study has several limitations. First, it was a single-center trial, which may limit generalizability. Future multicenter trials are needed to confirm the findings in diverse patient populations and healthcare settings. Second, the study population included only patients aged 18–75 years, so results may not apply to pediatric or elderly patients (≥ 75 years), who may have different risk profiles and responses to treatment. Third, we did not evaluate long-term effects beyond 30 days; future studies should assess the long-term impact of the intervention on respiratory function, quality of life, and recurrence of pulmonary complications. Fourth, the mechanistic substudy was limited to a small subset of patients (200 total), and we only measured a few key inflammatory cytokines and mucociliary function parameters. Larger mechanistic studies evaluating additional biomarkers such as oxidative stress markers, and mucin gene expression as well as more detailed assessments of mucociliary clearance (e.g., using scintigraphy) are needed to further elucidate the underlying mechanisms of action. Fifth, we did not collect data on patient adherence to the nebulization therapy, which may have influenced the results; future studies should include objective measures of adherence (e.g., nebulizer use logs, electronic monitoring devices). Sixth, the cost-effectiveness analysis was based on short-term costs (30 days postoperatively) and did not include long-term costs or indirect costs (e.g., lost productivity), which may affect the overall cost-effectiveness profile. Finally, while we stratified by tumor location, we did not consider other potential effect modifiers such as tumor size, histological type, or the extent of surgical resection, which may have influenced the intervention’s efficacy. The observed numerical differences in effect magnitude should be interpreted with caution. Future studies should explore these factors to identify more precise subgroups that may benefit most from the intervention.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, perioperative nebulized inhalation of budesonide combined with L-cysteine is an effective and safe intervention for reducing pulmonary complications in patients with posterior skull base tumors. This intervention exerts consistent protective effects across all tumor location subgroups, including the high-risk jugular vein region and foramen magnum subgroups. Multivariate analysis confirms that the combined nebulization therapy demonstrated a protective effect against pulmonary complications, and it can effectively mitigate the elevated pulmonary risk associated with intracranial nerve damage (the strongest independent risk factor identified), prolonged operative time, and prolonged mechanical ventilation. Additionally, the intervention improves postoperative respiratory function recovery (as evidenced by higher FVC and FEV₁ levels at 7 and 30 days postoperatively) and exhibits favorable cost-effectiveness, with lower total medical costs per patient and an ICER below the commonly accepted willingness-to-pay threshold. Mechanistic data further support the efficacy of this intervention by demonstrating reductions in airway inflammatory cytokines, decreased mucus viscosity, and improved mucociliary clearance. Given its favorable safety profile (no serious adverse events reported) and comprehensive benefits, perioperative nebulized budesonide with L-cysteine should be integrated into standard perioperative respiratory management for patients with posterior skull base tumors, particularly those at high risk. Future multicenter trials and long-term follow-up studies are warranted to validate these findings and explore optimal treatment protocols.
